odia: ଓଡ଼ିଆ ଢଗଢମାଳି ଚିହ୍ନା ଚିତ୍ର, ଛନ୍ଦ ଓ ଥଟ୍ଟାରେ ଦୈନନ୍ଦିନ ଜୀବନର କଥାକୁ ମନେ ରହିବା ପରି କହେ। ଲେମ୍ବୁ, ମେଘ ବା ଖାଲି ବଟୁଆର କଥା ଦେଇ କେବେ ପରାମର୍ଶ ଦିଆଯାଏ, କେବେ କାହାକୁ ଚିଡ଼ାଯାଏ, କେବେ ତାଙ୍କ ଆଚରଣ ନେଇ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ କରାଯାଏ। ଏହି ସଂଗ୍ରହରେ ଛନ୍ଦମୟ କଥନ, ପ୍ରବାଦ ଓ ଲକ୍ଷଣାର୍ଥରେ ବ୍ୟବହୃତ ଛୋଟ ଉକ୍ତି ରହିଛି; ସେମାନଙ୍କ ଭିନ୍ନ ରୂପ ଓ ବ୍ୟବହାରର ପ୍ରସଙ୍ଗକୁ ମଧ୍ୟ ଧ୍ୟାନ ଦିଆଯାଇଛି।
english: Odia dhaga–dhamali give everyday observations a memorable shape through familiar images, rhythm and pointed humour. A lemon, a cloud or an empty pouch can become a way to offer advice, tease someone or question their conduct. This collection brings together rhymed sayings, proverbs and figurative expressions, keeping their different forms and the situations in which they make sense in view.

entries.title: When too much turns bitter
entries.odia: ଅତି ଲେମ୍ବୁ ଚିପୁଡ଼ିଲେ ପିତା ।
entries.literal_meaning: If you squeeze a lemon too much, it turns bitter.
entries.explanation: The useful action—extracting juice—becomes counterproductive when carried too far. The warning is about proportion: pressing for one more favour, one more concession or one more advantage may damage what was already achieved. It does not mean that effort itself is bad.
entries.meaning_odia: ଅତି କଲେ ଭଲ କାମର ଫଳ ମଧ୍ୟ ଖରାପ ହୋଇପାରେ।
entries.usage_example: After a neighbour has agreed to help for an afternoon, repeatedly asking for more time may invite this saying. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The image makes a social judgement through an ordinary kitchen action. This reading explains the metaphor; it is not a scientific claim about every citrus fruit or a documented account of how the proverb originated.

entries.title: Inviting trouble
entries.odia: ଆ ବଳଦ ମୋତେ ବିନ୍ଧ ।
entries.literal_meaning: Come, ox, gore me.
entries.explanation: The speaker imagines someone summoning the very trouble they could have avoided. Used ironically, it criticises an unnecessary provocation or a knowingly risky decision. It should not be used to blame someone for harm they did not choose.

entries.cultural_context: ବଳଦ is rendered here as ox or bullock. The horned animal supplies the force of the image; the wording alone cannot establish a particular village, farming community or date of origin.

entries.title: There will be another winter
entries.odia: ଏକା ମାଘକେ ଶୀତ ଯାଏନାହିଁ।
entries.literal_meaning: Cold does not finish with a single Magha.
entries.explanation: One difficult season is not the last occasion on which we may need help. The saying can warn against treating a temporary advantage as permanent, or remind someone who refuses help that circumstances may change. Tone matters: it can sound like practical advice or a pointed warning.
entries.meaning_odia: ଆଜିର ଦରକାର ସରିଗଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଆଗକୁ ପୁଣି ଦରକାର ପଡ଼ିପାରେ।
entries.usage_example: After borrowing a tool successfully once, someone dismisses the neighbour who lent it. Another person reminds them that they may need that neighbour again. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: Magha supplies the seasonal image. The central point is recurring need and changing fortunes, not a precise forecast or a claim that cold is confined to one calendar month.

entries.title: Learning when responsibility arrives
entries.odia: କାନ୍ଧରେ ପଡିଲେ ବଜାଇ ଶିଖନ୍ତି
entries.literal_meaning: When it falls on the shoulder, one learns to play.
entries.explanation: Taking responsibility can force a beginner to learn the necessary skill. The compressed wording leaves the instrument unnamed; imagining a carried percussion instrument helps explain the metaphor, but does not establish which instrument first inspired it. This is encouragement to learn through doing, not a guarantee that preparation is unnecessary.
entries.meaning_odia: ଦାୟିତ୍ୱ ପଡ଼ିଲେ କାମ କରିବାର ଉପାୟ ଶିଖିହୁଏ।
entries.usage_example: A first-time organiser worries about arranging a neighbourhood reading session. A more experienced friend uses the saying while offering help with the practical tasks. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The body carrying a burden and the hands learning a performance meet in one image. No historical link to a named musical tradition has been verified.

entries.title: Not even a straw broken
entries.odia: କୁଟା ଖଣ୍ଡକ ଦିଖଣ୍ଡ ନ କରିବା
entries.literal_meaning: Not to break one piece of straw into two.
entries.explanation: This expression makes a very small action stand for any contribution at all. Saying that someone has not done even this means they have done no work in the situation being discussed. It is an idiomatic phrase rather than a complete rhymed maxim.
entries.meaning_odia: ସାମାନ୍ୟ କାମଟିଏ ମଧ୍ୟ ନ କରିବା।
entries.usage_example: Several people clean up after a gathering while one person only gives instructions. Someone complains that the person has not lifted a finger—the comparable English idiom. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: Straw provides a small, light object in the verbal image. The comparison with an English idiom explains the sense; it is not a claim of translation, borrowing or shared origin.

entries.title: Advice that stops at the doorstep
entries.odia: କହି ଦେଉଥାଇ ପରକୁ, ବୁଦ୍ଧି ନ ଦିଶଇ ଘରକୁ
entries.literal_meaning: One keeps advising others, but wisdom is not seen at home.
entries.explanation: The criticism is the gap between giving advice and practising it. The outward-facing adviser appears wise, yet fails to apply that wisdom to their own affairs. The saying invites self-examination; it does not imply that advice is worthless whenever its giver has difficulties.
entries.meaning_odia: ଅନ୍ୟକୁ ଉପଦେଶ ଦେଇ ନିଜେ ତାହା ନ ମାନିବା।
entries.usage_example: A person lectures everyone about keeping accounts but repeatedly loses track of their own spending. A relative uses this line to point out the inconsistency. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The rhyme of ପରକୁ and ଘରକୁ reinforces the contrast between others and home. Here the structure is part of the saying’s force, not just decoration.

entries.title: Noise is not the same as action
entries.odia: ଗରଜିଲା ମେଘ ବରଷେ ନାହିଁ
entries.literal_meaning: The cloud that thunders does not rain.
entries.explanation: The contrast between loud thunder and absent rain is used to question bluster: impressive promises or threats do not necessarily lead to action. Read the sentence figuratively. Thunderstorms can, of course, bring rain; the proverb is not a dependable weather rule.
entries.meaning_odia: ବଡ଼ ବଡ଼ କଥା କହିବା ଓ କାମ କରିବା ଏକ କଥା ନୁହେଁ।
entries.usage_example: Someone loudly promises to repair a shared bench, but nothing happens. Others use the saying to ask for action rather than another announcement. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: Weather becomes a way of talking about human speech. Similar imagery elsewhere would not by itself prove where this Odia wording originated.

entries.title: Planting when the meal is due
entries.odia: ବାହାଘର ବେଳେ ବାଇଗଣ ରୂଆ
entries.literal_meaning: Planting eggplant at wedding time.
entries.explanation: The joke is a mismatch between a long preparation and an immediate need. Planting a crop when the occasion has arrived cannot supply that occasion’s meal. The saying criticises starting essential work too late, rather than the act of planting itself.
entries.meaning_odia: ଦରକାର ବେଳ ଆସିଗଲା ପରେ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତି ଆରମ୍ଭ କରିବା।
entries.usage_example: The event starts tomorrow, but the organisers only now begin looking for a venue. Someone compares their timing to planting eggplant at wedding time. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The wedding and vegetable crop create the contrast. This does not prove eggplant is required at every Odia wedding or identify a particular community’s menu. The graphic illustrates lead time, not an agricultural timetable.

entries.title: Anger aimed at the bowl
entries.odia: ଓଷଦ ରାଗରେ ତାଟିଆ କାମୁଡିବା
entries.literal_meaning: Biting the bowl in anger at the medicine.
entries.explanation: The unpleasant thing is the medicine, but the anger is directed at its container. The expression describes displaced frustration: attacking a messenger, object or bystander instead of addressing the actual problem.
entries.meaning_odia: ଯାହା ପାଇଁ ରାଗ, ତାହା ବଦଳରେ ଅନ୍ୟ ଉପରେ ରାଗ ସୁଝାଇବା।
entries.usage_example: A delayed delivery frustrates a customer, who shouts at a neighbour merely passing on the update. Another person uses the saying to identify the misplaced anger. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The source writes ଓଷଦ and କାମୁଡିବା; this edition preserves those forms rather than silently replacing them with modern spellings. The image explains behaviour and gives no advice about taking medicine.

entries.title: A little game, an enormous quarrel
entries.odia: ଝିମିଟି ଖେଳରୁ ମହାଭାରତ

entries.explanation: A small disagreement grows into an outsized conflict. The Mahabharata provides a culturally recognisable scale of conflict. entries.cultural_context: ଝିମିଟି is retained rather than replaced by an invented modern game. The contrast is between a modest starting point and epic-scale escalation.

entries.title: When dishonest gain takes the roots with it
entries.odia: ଅଧର୍ମ ବିତ୍ତ ବଢେ ବହୁତ, ଗଲା ବେଳେ ଯାଏ ମୂଳ ସହିତ ।
entries.literal_meaning: Wrongfully gained wealth grows greatly, but disappears with its roots.
entries.explanation: The image contrasts rapid growth with loss at the root. Wealth obtained dishonestly may look impressive, yet the conduct behind it can endanger the whole household or enterprise. This is a moral warning about how gain is obtained, not a reliable prediction that every dishonest person will become poor.
entries.meaning_odia: ଅସତ୍ ଉପାୟରେ ଅର୍ଜିତ ଧନ ଶେଷରେ ସବୁ କିଛି ହରାଇବାର କାରଣ ହୋଇପାରେ।
entries.usage_example: A trader is tempted to falsify weights for a little extra profit. An older colleague uses the saying to warn that losing customers’ trust could destroy the business. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The rhyme of ବହୁତ and ସହିତ gives the warning a memorable close. The root image suggests losing the foundation, not merely the most recent gain. A version appears as the opening proverb of the1893 collection.

entries.title: Keeping one’s own dignity
entries.odia: ଆଲୋ ସଖି, ଆପଣା ମହତ ଆପେ ରଖି

entries.explanation: The friendly address makes this advice sound like one person speaking directly to another: preserve your dignity through your own conduct. entries.title: When praise becomes suspicious
entries.odia: ଅତି ଭକ୍ତି ଚୋର ଲକ୍ଷଣ ।
entries.literal_meaning: Excessive devotion is a thief’s sign.
entries.explanation: Exaggerated displays of devotion or deference can invite suspicion that the speaker wants something. In everyday use the warning can concern flattery, not only religious devotion. The force comes from the deliberately sharp word “thief”; the saying itself is not evidence that a particular admirer is dishonest.
entries.meaning_odia: ଅତ୍ୟଧିକ ତୋଷାମୋଦ ପଛରେ ସ୍ୱାର୍ଥ ଲୁଚିଥାଇପାରେ।
entries.usage_example: A stranger showers a shopkeeper with praise and then asks to take goods away without paying. The shopkeeper recalls this saying and checks the request carefully. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: ଭକ୍ତି supplies the outward appearance of reverence, while ଚୋର supplies the hidden motive in the proverb’s contrast. Interpretation depends on the conversation; sincere devotion is not being classified as theft.

entries.odia: ଅନ୍ଧାରରେ ବାଡ଼ି ବୁଲାଇବା ।
entries.literal_meaning: Swinging a stick in darkness.
entries.explanation: A stick swung in darkness may miss its intended target because the person cannot see where to aim. The expression describes guesses or effort without adequate information. Its criticism is not that no effort is being made, but that effort has no dependable direction.

entries.cultural_context: This is an idiomatic action phrase rather than a complete rhyming couplet. Darkness is the image for missing information; no specific origin incident has been established.

entries.title: An appetite larger than the means
entries.odia: ଅରଜି ନପାରେ ମୁଣ୍ଡ, ସୁଆଦ ଲୋଡୁଚି ତୁଣ୍ଡ ।
entries.literal_meaning: The head cannot earn; the mouth wants delicacies.
entries.explanation: The line sets the head’s inability to earn against the mouth’s demand for tasty food. It can rebuke expectations of luxury that do not match available means or contribution. Its tone is sharp and can be hurtful when applied to someone whose circumstances are outside their control.

entries.title: Spending tomorrow’s means today
entries.odia: ଆଜି କୁରୁ କୁରୁ ହସୁ, କାଲି ଲଙ୍ଗଳ କାହିଁରେ ଚଷୁ ?
entries.literal_meaning: Today you laugh merrily; tomorrow, what will you plough with?
entries.explanation: The teasing question asks what will remain after today’s enjoyment. It warns against consuming the very means needed for tomorrow’s work. The pleasure is immediate, while the cost becomes visible only when work must resume.

entries.odia: ଆରେ ଏ, ଯେତେବେଳେ ଯେ

entries.explanation: This compressed expression advises a fitting response to the circumstances. It may interrupt someone who insists on handling every situation in the same way. The point is practical judgement about this occasion, rather than a rule that commitments can always be discarded.

entries.title: A welcome that sends you away
entries.odia: ଆସିଲ ବନ୍ଧୁ ଭଲ କଲ, ବସିବାକୁ ନାହିଁ ଠା, ଯେଉଁ ବାଟେ ବାଟେ ଆସିଲ ବନ୍ଧୁ ସେଇ ବାଟେ ବାଟେ ଯା ।
entries.literal_meaning: Good of you to come, friend; there is nowhere to sit. Go back by the very way you came.
entries.explanation: The opening sounds hospitable, but the ending cancels the welcome. The humour lies in that sudden reversal: someone offers warm words while making it plain that the visitor is unwanted. Used pointedly, it exposes courtesy that provides no actual welcome.

entries.cultural_context: The repeated address to a friend sharpens the irony. The example extends that verbal pattern to another setting; no historical hospitality custom is being asserted.

entries.title: Value put to the test
entries.odia: କାଚ, କାଚ, ମଣି, ମଣି, କିଣା ବିକା ବେଳେ ଜଣା ଜଣି

entries.title: Nodding without understanding

entries.title: Refusing to be polished into something else
entries.odia: ମୋତେ ଯେତେ ମାଠିବୁ ମାଠ ମୁହିଁ ସେଇ ଦରପଡ଼ା କାଠ
entries.literal_meaning: Polish me as much as you like; I remain that half-burnt wood.
entries.explanation: The speaker declares that repeated efforts to change or improve them will not work. The blunt material image can make the refusal comic, defiant or self-deprecating. It voices a stance in a conversation, not a truth that people cannot learn or change.
entries.meaning_odia: ଯେତେ ବୁଝାଇଲେ ବା ବଦଳାଇବାକୁ ଚେଷ୍ଟା କଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ନିଜେ ସେପରି ରହିବି ବୋଲି କହିବା।
entries.usage_example: After repeated advice to adopt a more fashionable manner, someone jokingly insists that they will remain as they are. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The wood image and the first-person voice are preserved. This is distinct from enduring pressure: here the emphasis falls on resisting another person’s attempts to remake the speaker. entries.literal_meaning: Even if the dhinki goes to heaven, it will still pound paddy.
entries.explanation: The joke gives a rice-pounding implement a grand change of address but leaves its work exactly as before. In conversation, it can tease someone who brings an old habit into a new setting, or express frustration that a change of place has changed nothing. The pointed contrast is between heaven and the same everyday task.

entries.title: The fire nobody sees

entries.literal_meaning: When a forest burns, the world knows; when the heart burns, no one knows.
entries.explanation: Visible calamity draws attention; private grief can remain unnoticed. The contrast asks the listener to recognise pain that has no outward blaze.

entries.literal_meaning: For an uncomprehending king, a bundle-of-straw minister.
entries.explanation: Poor leadership is compounded by equally foolish advice. The pairing, rather than the ruler alone, is the target.
entries.meaning_odia: ନେତା ବୁଝୁନାହାନ୍ତି, ତାଙ୍କ ପରାମର୍ଶଦାତା ମଧ୍ୟ ଠିକ୍ ବୁଦ୍ଧି ଦେଇପାରୁନାହାନ୍ତି—ଦୁଇଜଣଙ୍କ ଯୋଗରେ ଅସୁବିଧା ବଢ଼େ।

entries.title: Each place has its own ways

entries.title: One hand cannot clap
entries.odia: ଏକା ହାତରେ ତାଳି ବାଜେ ନାହିଁ

entries.odia: ଆଳୁ ଖୋଳୁ ଖୋଳୁ ମହାଦେବ ବାହାରିଲେ
entries.literal_meaning: While digging for tubers, Mahadeva appeared.
entries.explanation: An ordinary investigation unexpectedly brings a much larger matter to light. This explanation follows the contrast in scale; the dictionary does not provide an origin tale.
entries.meaning_odia: ସାଧାରଣ କିଛି ଖୋଜୁ ଖୋଜୁ ଅପ୍ରତ୍ୟାଶିତ ଭାବେ ବଡ଼ କଥା ବାହାରି ପଡ଼ିବା। ଛୋଟ ଖୋଜାରୁ ବଡ଼ ଆବିଷ୍କାର—ଏହି ବିପରୀତତାରେ କଥାଟିର ମଜା।
entries.usage_example: Checking one unexplained receipt reveals a much larger error in the accounts. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The source labels it ଢଗ under appearing or becoming visible. Mahadeva is Shiva; no particular excavated shrine, village or historical discovery is verified.

entries.title: When silence is read as agreement
entries.odia: ମୌନଂ ସମ୍ମତିଲକ୍ଷଣଂ
entries.literal_meaning: Silence is a sign of agreement.
entries.explanation: This maxim describes an inference people make from another person’s silence. Silence can also mean hesitation, fear or uncertainty, so it does not establish that someone has agreed.
entries.meaning_odia: ଚୁପ୍ ରହିବାକୁ ସମ୍ମତିର ଚିହ୍ନ ବୋଲି ଧରାଯାଉଥିବା ଧାରଣାକୁ ଏହି କଥାଟି କହେ। କିନ୍ତୁ ଭୟ, ଦ୍ୱିଧା ବା ଅନିଶ୍ଚୟରେ ବି ମଣିଷ ଚୁପ୍ ରହିପାରେ; ସମ୍ମତି ନିଶ୍ଚିତ କରିବାକୁ ସ୍ପଷ୍ଟ ଉତ୍ତର ଦରକାର।
entries.usage_example: A chair assumes the quiet room approves a plan; a participant asks for an explicit response from everyone. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
entries.cultural_context: The dictionary identifies a Sanskrit maxim. It is documented here as an expression to examine, not permission to treat silence as consent.
